newsitem.title: THAILAND: IMF gives Laos pat on the back on economy.
newsitem.headline: IMF gives Laos pat on the back on economy.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund's resident representative in impoverished Laos on Wednesday gave the country a pat on the back for launching sound economic reforms this year.
The IMF's Paul Wade said a mission from the agency's Washington headquarters had visited Laos last week and found that economic reforms in the communist nation so far this year to be positive.

"The mid-term review of the third annual arrangement of the ESAF (Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility) programme is quite favourable," he told Reuters by telephone from the Laotian capital of Vientiane.
Tiny, land-locked Laos has 4.5 million people and an annual per capita income of US$350.
"On the macroeconomic front, the government has undertaken policies which are broadly sound and good. There has been a strong economic performance this year," he said.
Especially notable was a drop in monthly inflation rates, which fell to a low 4.5 percent at the end of August from 27 and 29 percent in January and February.
"On the inflation rate, it's very good news," he said. Inflation jumped to 19 percent at end-1995 from 6.7 percent in 1994. The government hopes the rate will fall to 12 percent this year.
The Laotian kip depreciated in value after inflation soared, dipping to 930 against the U.S. dollar in the second half of 1995 from 720 in the first half of the year.

Wade said the government had also maintained high economic growth, and the IMF was confident that earlier predictions of a 7.5 percent growth in the gross domestic product (GDP) would continue through 1996, up from 7.1 percent in 1995.
"We see that growth continues to be high at 7.5 percent. We are quite happy with that," he said.
The IMF estimate is slightly higher than that of the Laotian Ministry of Finance, which in mid-September predicted GDP growth for 1996 would reach 7.1 percent.
The Laotian economy nearly collapsed after experimenting with socialist policies in the mid-1980s. Then the cash-strapped government introduced new reforms aimed at moving towards a market economy.
The government has since liberalised exchange rate policies, strictly controlled by the central bank in the past, by allowing commercial banks to set their own independent rates.

The authorities have also increased revenues for the national budget and encouraged higher cash crop production to raise incomes. Export duties have been scrapped on commodities to help balance outflows from the import-dependent economy.
Finance Minister Saysomphone Phomvihane told Reuters earlier this month that Laos was strongly committed to continuing strict implementation of the reforms.
The IMF started assistance for Laos in 1989 with a three-year loan programme. The last disbursement from the $54 million loan is scheduled for next November, Wade said.

"We feel that the macroeconomic policies (undertaken from the start of IMF's involvement in 1989) have been broadly successful in stabilising the economy and structural reforms have been in steady progress," he said.

Wade said that because "the track record for the Laotian government is encouraging," it was likely that the IMF would continue cooperation with Laos after its funding programme ends next May. He said no final decision had yet been taken.
